title: Three implementation details behind a local-LLM interrogation game in Unity
author: Comfortable-Cat-9611
selftext:
I made The Interview, a small Unity scene where you question a character in your own words, compare answers against a dossier and decide whether to clear or detain them. The conversation runs locally using Qwen3, Whisper and Piper. I also sell the Unity toolkit underneath it; I checked this post with the mods, and this write-up is about implementation ideas you can use independently of that toolkit.



The first detail is the streaming callback. In the LLMforUnity integration I used, each callback contains the entire reply so far, not just the new characters. If the callbacks are "I", "I came", "I came yesterday.", appending all three produces repeated text, which can then get spoken aloud. The parser needs to remember what it has consumed and extract only the new tail. At generation end, I also pass the final returned text through the parser and flush the remaining fragment. Otherwise a last sentence without punctuation can disappear from the voice output. A simple length cursor works for an append-only stream; if your provider can rewrite earlier text, you also need prefix checks and a policy for text that has already been spoken.



The second detail is that there are two speech queues. Finished text units go into a synthesis queue; completed audio clips go into a playback queue. Piper produces a WAV for each unit. While sentence A plays, sentence B can be synthesized and the LLM can still be generating sentence C. This overlaps work that would otherwise happen sequentially. It is sentence-level pipelining, not continuously streamed audio from individual tokens.



Splitting on every period is too crude: abbreviations, decimal numbers and trailing quotation marks need attention. Very short fragments can be merged, and a maximum unit size helps when the model keeps writing without punctuation. Subtitles should follow the unit actually being played; connecting them directly to the newest generated text lets them race ahead of the voice. Cancellation also has to cover both queues and the currently playing clip, or an old sentence can arrive after the conversation has ended.



The third detail is where the game rules live. In this demo, the player marks dossier statements and makes the CLEAR/DETAIN decision through the game UI. An NPC saying "you can let me through" does not itself change that result. More generally, if you want generated actions, treat them as requests: parse an allowed action and target, check them in your game code, then call a handler you explicitly implemented. Structured output helps with the format; it does not make the character's claims true or replace gameplay validation.



For latency, measure separate stages: end of player input, transcript ready, first complete text unit, and first audible sample. A TTS timer starting when a sentence is queued leaves out recognition and the wait for that sentence. Cold model loading is another separate cost. Typing a question is a useful way to isolate the voice-input part when comparing runs on the same machine.



The free English Windows demo is here: [https://merrymaker14.itch.io/the-interview](https://merrymaker14.itch.io/the-interview)

The game download is about 788 MB, with an additional model download during initial setup. It runs locally after that setup; response speed depends on the hardware and selected model.



Project website and documentation, for context: [https://merrymaker14.github.io/offline-ai-npc/](https://merrymaker14.github.io/offline-ai-npc/)



If you have built a spoken NPC, how do you choose the point at which a partial reply is ready to speak? I am particularly interested in the trade-off between short first fragments and more natural phrasing.



Disclosure: AI assisted with preparing this English write-up from my project notes and implementation.
